item.title: Why Some People Lurk But Never Like
item.description:
Social Media

Why Some People Lurk But Never Like

Online lurking can feel very different depending on which platform it happens on.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Lurking can reflect curiosity, caution, comparison, or fear rather than disengagement.
  • Silent social media use can be psychologically active even when it leaves no visible trace.
  • Lurkers' motivations and outcomes may depend on the platform they use most often.
  • Instagram invites lifestyle comparison, for instance, while LinkedIn encourages professional comparison.

Some people appear to know everything that happens on social media while revealing almost nothing about themselves. They seem to watch every Instagram story, notice who has changed jobs on LinkedIn, or remember photographs that others have forgotten posting.

Yet they rarely click “like,” leave a comment, or publish anything themselves. They are socially present but digitally invisible. This behaviour is often described as lurking: consuming social media content without visibly engaging with it.

Why Do People Lurk Online?

Although the word can sound secretive, lurking has no single psychological explanation. A person may remain silent because they are curious, cautious, socially anxious, professionally strategic, or simply uninterested in performing their life online. Someone may follow a university colleague on LinkedIn to learn about publication opportunities without announcing their presence. Another person may watch an old friend’s Instagram stories because it creates a subtle sense of connection, even though they have not spoken for months.

Researchers commonly distinguish between active social media use, such as posting, commenting, and messaging, and passive use, such as scrolling. However, this distinction can be deceptive. Someone may spend seconds posting a photograph, while a silent viewer might compare, interpret, and remember it for hours.

A review of 141 studies found that active and passive use were not strongly associated with most aspects of well-being; their effects depended on the person, context and activity involved (Godard and Holtzman, 2024). Visible engagement is not the same as psychological involvement.

For some people, lurking is self-protection. Posting exposes us to evaluation: A photograph may receive fewer likes than expected, an opinion may be challenged, or a comment may be misunderstood.

Imagine someone writing a LinkedIn post about leadership, rereading it repeatedly and deleting it because a senior colleague might disagree. The imagined audience becomes more powerful than the desire to speak. Silence allows the person to benefit from the platform without accepting the risks of visibility.

Perfectionism can produce a similar pattern. A woman may take photographs throughout a holiday but post none because they seem less impressive than the images already filling her Instagram feed. A lecturer may want to share an achievement on LinkedIn but decide that it appears insignificant beside a colleague’s promotion or major grant. When the standard for participation becomes impossibly high, observation replaces expression. Others lurk to learn. A new academic, for example, may observe how established researchers announce publications and respond to criticism before deciding how to present themselves.

Lurking on Instagram vs. LinkedIn: How the Platform Changes Psychology

The psychology of lurking also varies across platforms. Comparing Instagram and LinkedIn, specifically, is revealing because lurking is common on both but can serve different purposes.

Instagram centres largely on visual and personal self-presentation. Users encounter carefully selected bodies, relationships, homes, restaurants, and holidays. Someone scrolling after an exhausting day might see an engagement announcement, then an influencer’s seemingly perfect body, then a former colleague in an expensive hotel. The mind can combine these separate moments into one impossible conclusion: Everyone else is attractive, loved, wealthy, and enjoying life.

This can encourage upward social comparison—that is, comparing ourselves with people who appear to be doing better. Research links social comparison and envy on social networking platforms with poorer well-being, although the effect differs among users (Carraturo et al., 2023). A marathon photograph might inspire one observer while reminding another of an abandoned goal.

Overall, research has found that while some people feel worse after browsing, others feel better, and many experience little change (Valkenburg et al., 2022). Passive use is not automatically harmful; much depends on what people view and how they interpret it.

LinkedIn, by contrast, produces a more professional form of comparison. Instead of bodies, relationships, and holidays, users tend to compare promotions, publications, awards, and new positions. Someone satisfied with their career in the morning may feel behind after 10 minutes of reading polished success stories.

Instagram can provoke the question, “Why doesn’t my life look like that?” LinkedIn asks, “Why am I not further ahead?” Posting there may also feel riskier because employers, colleagues, students, clients, and recruiters can occupy the same audience. Silence may therefore be strategic rather than anxious; the individual is managing reputational risk.

The Emotional Downside of Lurking on Social Media

Lurking can become psychologically costly when it repeatedly leaves someone feeling inferior, excluded, or powerless. One person might check a former partner’s Instagram account every night despite feeling distressed. Another might monitor colleagues’ LinkedIn achievements until every success feels like evidence of personal failure.

The problem in those cases is not their failure to post. It is that observation has stopped being intentional and become a cycle of comparison, avoidance or emotional self-punishment.

A healthier relationship with social media does not require becoming a content creator. It may begin with two questions: “What am I looking for?” and “How do I feel after finding it?”

If particular accounts repeatedly generate envy or inadequacy, changing the feed may help more than merely measuring screen time. If fear of judgment prevents desired participation, a private message or thoughtful comment may be an easier beginning than a public post.

People who lurk are not absent from social media. They form its invisible audience, silently but consistently interpreting what others display. Their reticence may reflect caution, curiosity, comparison, affection or fear.

In short, online silence is not empty. Sometimes it is peaceful, sometimes strategic, and sometimes it carries more psychological activity than any visible post.

item.title: The More Your Adult Child Panics, the More You Pay
item.description:
Parenting

The More Your Adult Child Panics, the More You Pay

How repeated financial rescues teach an adult child that urgency gets results.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Urgency in financial crises can condition families to rely on panic for quick fixes.
  • Fast monetary rescues reinforce adult children's dependency.
  • Healthy support responds to the problem, not just the panic.

I hear this so often from the parents who reach out to me. The rent is due tomorrow, or the car won’t start, and you've got to love this one: The credit card is maxed out. The same mess, different day, where your adult child calls sounding frightened, overwhelmed, or desperate. You hear the urgency in their voice, and suddenly this isn’t merely a financial decision. It feels like an emergency, and there is a part of you that does not want to once again put on that first responder uniform. Yet you quickly send the money, anyway. So that problem is now solved—or is it?

The Entire Family Can Become Dependent on the Crisis

One of the most overlooked risks of repeatedly rescuing an adult child financially is not simply that they may become dependent on the money. Here’s what I usually hear about how it goes down. Urgency activates a parent’s protective system. Yes, we are talking about the reacting part of your brain going into full alert status. Your adult child is distressed, so you become distressed. The pressure builds until somebody does something, so then you Venmo $600. Truly amazing times we live in because those quick presses on your phone lead to your adult child feeling relief within seconds, and so do you.

That relief is psychologically powerful because it teaches both people something: When the distress gets high enough, money makes it stop. Nobody deliberately created that rule. Yet repeated enough times, it can become the family’s unofficial financial policy.

“Just This Once” So Often Turns Into Another “Just This Once”

In my book Mom, Dad… I Promise I’ll Pay You Back: The One-Day Reset to Encourage Independence Without Pushing Your Adult Child Away, I describe how financial decisions between parents and adult children often carry emotions far bigger than the dollar amount. Money can represent safety, love, fear, reassurance, and even proof that a parent hasn’t abandoned their child. The trouble starts when urgency drives the decision.

But let's hold on a minute, slow down, and now consider two very different responses to the same request. One is immediate and goes something like the parent saying, “Okay, okay. How much do you need?” The other hits the pause button on the emotional machinery and sounds way different: “I hear that you’re really worried. Let’s figure out what happened and what your options are before we decide what help makes sense.”

Notice that the second response isn’t rejection, as it is still loving. But that second response, with the reflective pause and collaborative tone, separates responding to distress from automatically financing it. That distinction matters because adult independence requires something uncomfortable: opportunities to tolerate problems long enough to solve them.

Parents Need Tolerance Too

Sometimes the hardest part of changing a financial pattern isn’t watching your adult child become uncomfortable. Rather, it’s tolerating your own discomfort while they do. So before responding to the next urgent request as a SWAT team leader and a full-on rescue of your adult child, simply ask yourself: If this exact problem were presented calmly instead of as a crisis, would I make the same financial decision? That question may seem obvious, but trust me, amid the crisis texts and calls parents receive, the obvious often goes out the window. And please realize that if your answer is no, then you have just realized that the sense of urgency may be making the decision for you. And who makes the decision, based on the reality of the situation, may be most of how you respond.

Final Thoughts

Let me reiterate one more time. I am not against parents financially helping out their adult children. But when panic becomes the driving force of a repetitive dysfunctional rescue pattern, which I, in a prior post, termed Rescue-Entitlement-Dependency (R.E.D), then the adult child ends up stagnating in developing independence.

item.title: The Madness of the Modern World
item.description:
Stress

The Madness of the Modern World

Could society actually be too much for us to handle?

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • We have not evolved to cope with modern life.
  • We face too much input from too many directions, and we are overloaded.
  • Key environments need to change to better meet our psychological needs.
Source: Brian Merrill / Pixabay

There is something I have known for a long time, something that clients are increasingly bringing into their sessions with me, and something that needs to be written about way more often than it currently is. And it’s this: All the stress, all the exhaustion, all the mental health issues; it’s not you. It is not your fault. It’s not even your responsibility. Basically, our brains just aren’t built to handle modern life. They have not evolved enough to cope with the constant demands, distractions, and decisions that our societies contain, involve, and heap upon us each and every single day. And finally, psychological research is saying it too.

A recent meta-analysis, published in the journal Behavioural Sciences, highlights a rather large evolutionary mismatch between the environments we human beings actually evolved for and the environments we currently find ourselves in. Perhaps unsurprisingly, this mismatch is causing many of our mental health problems. Our brains and our bodies are still hunter-gatherer brains and bodies, only they haven’t been living the hunt-and-gather lifestyle for many thousands of years. 1

What we evolved for

We were made for small close-knit groups of people (our tribe); immediate physical threats that were over quickly (sabre-toothed tigers); gentle stimulation from the natural world (think of the wind rustling the leaves on the trees and the water gently babbling in the brook); together with cooperative rituals that involved chanting, singing, dancing, communal eating, and such like.

What we are dealing with

We were not designed for huge teeming cities, vast digital networks (full of social comparison and one-upmanship); nebulous and never-ending threats (climate change, cost-of-living crises, geopolitical instabilities, AI, and more); overstimulation and sensory bombardment (bright lights, TV screens, laptops, mobile phones, short-form content, etc.); and solitary (and often screen-based) living (no wonder there’s a loneliness epidemic).

Stop the world

The review, from social scientists and psychologists in Singapore, confirms that we are all overwhelmed, and that modern life is pushing our poor, beleaguered minds way beyond their already overtaxed limits. Hence the rise in diagnoses of anxiety, stress, depression, and more.

The researchers involved refer to the current clutch of disparate calamities we are all dealing with here in good old 2026 as a "polycrisis" (which is way more polite than what I’ve been calling it). Together they are increasing the risk of burnout and reducing our overall well-being.

Whilst none of the maladies of modern life are your responsibility, managing your stress issues as effectively as you can sadly sits within your domain. But it’s not just down to you. It’s no good paying a fortune to manage your stress if you keep returning to the environments that are stressing you out.

The authors suggest that everything needs an overhaul. And they mean everything. Cities, workplaces, digital platforms—basically every system and environment—could all be redesigned in ways that better suit our psychological needs. They point to more green spaces (always a good thing), less overwhelming urban environments (again with the yes), and more could all help improve our mental health.

It might sound obvious, but it’s also revolutionary. If modern life were not so stressful, we would not be so stressed.

Whilst on the subject

Another problem with our human brains is that they were also not built for happiness. Instead, they were built for survival. Again, this goes back to hunter-gatherer times.

Back then (back then being a couple of hundred thousand years or so ago), you’d break camp in the morning and off you would trot, there to either hunt or gather. And sure, it might be nice, as you returned to camp at the end of the day, to talk about the nice time you had picking berries and hunting gazelle, but really, you needed to talk about the dangers that you faced or noticed.

There were short-term dangers (back to those pesky sabre-toothed tigers) and long-term dangers (harsh winters). If you didn’t focus on those dangers, your tribe could die.

But fast-forward to the modern world. We still break camp in the morning, metaphorically hunting and gathering our day away, only the dangers we bring home are far more numerous (traffic jams, poor performance reviews, and such like) and far more nebulous (back to those polycrises).

The definitive study on this whole "we were built to focus on danger" angle was published in the Review of General Psychology back in 2001. In it, the researchers said that the human brain was evolutionarily built to prioritise survival over positive emotional states. And so, we focus on the bad before we can even consider the good. Thankfully, that hardwired habit can be reversed. 2

The trick of it here is to go against the grain of that evolutionary brain and focus on the positive. It isn’t easy. It takes lots of practice. But, at the end of each working day, you can bring home the things that went well, the things that you got right, and the things that made you happy.

Whilst this will help you to focus on the positive more than the negative (and therefore be a good thing for your well-being), it sadly doesn’t fix the constant bombardment that we face from daily life in the 21st century.

For that, you might want to sit in a forest for a good long while. Try pretending that it’s 250,000 years ago. Only, don’t forget to turn your phone off.

item.title: How Nolan Wells and Tyler Smith Stir Black Mistrust
item.description:
Race and Ethnicity

How Nolan Wells and Tyler Smith Stir Black Mistrust

Recent deaths show why racial socialization in Black families still matters.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Black families’ mistrust of official narratives is rooted in historical and contemporary experiences.
  • Racial socialization teaches Black youth how to navigate being “the only one” in White social spaces.
  • Cultural mistrust is not irrational; it is a survival strategy shaped by Black lived experience.

On July 4, 18-year-old Nolan Wells died somewhere off the shoreline of Horn Island, Mississippi, while boating with his friends. This tragic story would not have sparked national attention but for the fact that Nolan was Black and his friends were White. Against the backdrop of Mississippi with its painful and violent racial history, many Black people are understandably concerned and distressed about this case.

Meanwhile, in Lexington, Kentucky, 18-year-old Tyler Jay Smith was attending a gathering on July 4 with his peers. Police were later called to the scene, where they found Tyler had a gunshot to the face. Tyler died on July 5. This tragic story has not generated the amount of national attention as the Nolan Wells case, but one fact is constant: Tyler was Black and his peers were White. Like Nolan’s family, Tyler’s family is devastated.

Why Official Narratives Fail to Reassure Black Families

In both cases, there are more questions than answers regarding the specific details surrounding the mysterious deaths, and both families have grave concerns about the handling of the cases. Among other things, the Wells family is concerned that the cause and manner of Nolan’s death could not be determined by an independent autopsy, and that drowning could not be determined because his lungs had been removed during the state’s autopsy (which is customary). Tyler’s family is concerned that the Lexington police immediately labeled the shooting “accidental and self-inflicted” when evidence was allegedly tampered with.

The purpose of this post is not to litigate the facts of these cases in a public forum. Hopefully all of the facts will eventually be uncovered, and justice, if needed, will be meted out.

Speculation on social media has run rampant among Black people. For example, there is a TikTok video indicating that Nolan’s autopsy revealed deep tissue discoloration in the back of his head (confirmed) and an alleged missing neck bone (which is not confirmed), while other videos allege that his hyoid bone was broken. The rampant speculation on Black social media reflects a pervasive mistrust among Black people toward White-owned media to care about, or accurately report, the deaths of Black people under questionable circumstances.

Racial Socialization as a Framework for Understanding Responses

In Black families, communication about race is central to how many parents socialize their children. Racial socialization is the intergenerational process by which Black parents and families teach Black youth about their culture, the significance of race, and how to navigate a society marked by racial inequities and the devaluation of Blackness. Black psychologists have provided foundational scholarship on the importance of racial socialization.

Racial socialization is often thought of in the context of racism and policing (i.e., “The Talk” that Black youth, especially Black males, receive from their parents). However, the deaths of Nolan Wells and Tyler Jay Smith underscore the racial socialization that takes place in messages about being the only Black person interacting and socializing with White peers and friends, especially the promotion of interracial mistrust. It is important to understand why the promotion of interracial mistrust (which usually means cultural mistrust of White people) is so prevalent in Black social media and in the racial socialization messages of Black parents.

Intergenerational Narratives and Cultural Mistrust

The promotion of cultural mistrust of White people can be attributed, in part, to the stories shared intergenerationally in Black families about racial or racist incidents that become part of family lore. When I was growing up as a young Black kid in Pilot Mountain, North Carolina, during the 1970s and 1980s, my parents told my siblings and me a story about our cousin who went hiking with his White high school classmates in Sauratown Mountains. As the story goes, our cousin “slipped” and fell off the mountain to his death, while his classmates all returned unscathed. Of course, my parents (like many Black people of their generation) did not believe that he just slipped. They suspected foul play was involved. The message and lesson they conveyed to us was that we should avoid situations where we were the only Black person, for fear that something untoward could happen to us. This story has stayed with me my entire life.

Stories like this, and the countless numbers of mysterious, unexplained, and unaccounted for deaths of Black people in this country, have become part of the collective psyche of Black people. Black folks are often criticized for being hypervigilant around issues of race, accused of “playing the race card,” and always seeing ourselves as victims. Additionally, Black folks have historically had a tendency to distrust White people, leading two Black psychiatrists to argue that Black people needed to develop a “healthy” cultural paranoia to survive in America.

A recent TikTok video fed the conspiratorial conjecture and cultural mistrust of Black people when a White man mocked the death of Nolan Wells, smiling and saying provocative statements like “We sure did do it,” “What you think we do when we take y’all young men camping with us?” “We know them boys don’t know how to swim,” “They did it, them boys did it,” “This is the damn tradition,” “You know every six months we, this skin tone, we all get together in our neighborhoods, and we have like a neighborhood meeting, and y’all ain’t invited,” “We make plans, we talk about y’all….”

While it is not clear whether he was being sarcastic or serious, it was clear from the almost 10,000 comments that most Black people believed he was not joking and was telling the truth. Many Black people saw it as a confession.

We don’t know what happened to Nolan Wells and Tyler Jay Smith. But Black families do know the violent racial history of this country, and some are understandably nervous and mistrustful when their Black children are the only Black individuals in White social outings. This is a sad commentary but unfortunately reflects the lived experiences of Black people in this country.
